findings.title: Exhausted recovery-code credentials stored in user storage are never removed
findings.body: After a successful recovery-code login, the authenticator now looks up the credential with the new federated-aware RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(), so the returned credential may live in user storage. However, when all codes are used it still calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...), which only deletes credentials from Keycloak's local store. For a credential supplied by a user storage provider this call silently no-ops: the exhausted credential remains in the user storage, isConfiguredFor()/configuredFor() keep returning true, and getCredential() keeps returning the used-up credential. The only recovery path is the required action being added afterwards; if the user abandons that flow, the stale credential persists and there is no code path that ever cleans it up (the class never attempts disableCredentialType or updateCredential on the provider for the exhausted credential). The removal should handle the federated case (or the all-codes-used branch should be skipped/handled differently for credentials whose ID belongs to a user storage provider).

findings.title: getCredential prefers federated over local, but isValid validates local credentials first
findings.body: The new getCredential() checks getFederatedCredentialsStream() first and only falls back to locally stored credentials. UserCredentialManager.isValid(), however, validates against locally stored credentials before delegating to user storage. If a user ends up with both a local and a federated recovery-codes credential (e.g. had local codes and is later linked to a user storage that also reports the type), the code that validated successfully may be the local one, while the post-validation bookkeeping in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator (allCodesUsed() check, removal of the exhausted credential, triggering CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES) operates on the federated credential. The exhausted local credential would then never be detected or removed. This is also a behavior change on upgrade: an existing local recovery-codes credential is now shadowed by any federated one, whereas before only local credentials were consulted.

findings.title: New recovery-keys test does not verify one-time-use semantics or the exhausted-credential path
findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only performs a single successful login with the first recovery code. It never asserts that reusing the same code fails, never requests a second code to verify the displayed code number advances, and never exercises the 'all codes used' branch (removal of the credential and re-triggering of the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action) for a user-storage-backed credential. Notably, the test storage provider's isValid() accepts ANY of the stored raw codes regardless of the number shown on the login page and never marks a code as used, so even a broken implementation that ignores the requested code number or never consumes codes would pass this test. Given that the all-codes-used cleanup is exactly the part that does not work for federated credentials (removeStoredCredentialById is local-only), this path should be covered.

findings.title: getCredentials() dereferences myUser without null check
findings.body: The newly added getCredentials(RealmModel, UserModel) calls getMyUser(user) and immediately accesses myUser.recoveryCodes and myUser.otp. getMyUser() can return null when the user is not present in the in-memory map (other methods in the same class, e.g. isConfiguredFor() and isValid(), explicitly guard against this). A call for an unknown user — e.g. from admin/account credential listing or UserCredentialManager.getFederatedCredentialsStream() during edge-case lookups — would throw a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty stream.
